# The Last Watch of the Mara Celeste

---

People ask me how a person drowns on purpose and I tell them: she didn't drown on purpose. She just refused to leave. There's a difference, though I couldn't tell you where it lives.

---

My name is Dora Saldanha. I cooked aboard the *Mara Celeste* for eleven years, first for Captain Wen's grandfather, old Joaquim, and then for Wen herself after the cancer took him quick and mean in the January of '09. I made fish stew and black coffee and rice with egg and whatever else the sea gave us or the port towns sold cheap. I am not a hero of this story. I am the woman who made tea.

---

Let me tell you about the boat first.

She was a sixty-two-foot coastal freighter, wooden-hulled, built in 1971 at a yard in Figueira da Foz that doesn't exist anymore. Her planking was angelim pedra — ironwood — and old Joaquim used to say she'd outlast every one of us and he was almost right. She had a two-cylinder diesel that sounded like a man coughing in a cathedral. She smelled of salt and diesel and linseed oil and the particular funk of a bilge that has been alive longer than some countries.

She was not worth much money. That is important for you to understand.

What she was worth, in dollars, was less than what the bank said Wen owed on the second mortgage she'd taken against the boat to pay for the first mortgage she'd taken against the boat to pay for old Joaquim's treatments that didn't work. I didn't understand the arithmetic of it then and I don't now. What I understood was the letters. They came to every port. They found us in Bridgetown and Scarborough and once, God help us, in a village in Dominica that didn't have paved roads, and still the letters came, printed on paper so white it hurt to look at.

Wen read them at the galley table and folded them back along their creases and put them in a coffee tin she kept under her bunk.

I never once saw her cry over them. I also never once saw her smile after they started. I want you to hold those two facts together.

---

The repo men. Yes. Let me tell that part.

We'd gotten word — Wen had gotten word, through a friend in Hamilton who worked the harbor office — that Maritime Asset Recovery Associates, whatever soulless birth produced that name, had filed papers in Bermuda and had a team standing by to seize the *Mara Celeste* the moment she docked. We were three days out of Hamilton, carrying a hold of dried goods and canned fruit for a grocery wholesaler who'd paid half up front.

Wen came down to the galley and sat across from me and said, "Dora, we're not going to Bermuda."

I said, "Then where?"

She didn't answer for a while. She picked up the deck of cards we kept in the tin cup nailed to the shelf and shuffled them, that particular shuffle she had where she bridged them high and let them waterfall, a sound like small rain.

"South," she said.

"There's nothing south."

"There's sea."

That was Tuesday.

---

I need to talk about the card game.

Every morning, six o'clock, before the crew was up, Wen and I played rummy at the galley table. This was a tradition older than my employment. Old Joaquim had played with his cook, a man named Beto who I replaced when his knees gave out, and when Wen inherited the boat she inherited the game, and when I sat down across from her that first morning she dealt without asking whether I knew the rules.

Eleven years. I estimate roughly three thousand games. She won more than I did because she remembered every card I picked up and every card I put down, and she'd look at me over her hand with those eyes — dark and flat as coffee in a mug — and she'd know what I was holding before I knew it myself.

We never played for money. We played for first choice of the fruit at breakfast. A small thing. A stupid thing. I tell you about it because when the world was ending we were still playing cards, and I don't know what that means except that maybe the world only ends if you agree to let it.

---

The typhoon.

It was not supposed to be there. This is the Sargasso, you understand — the dead water, the place where the weed grows thick as carpet and the current runs in its great slow circle and nothing much happens. Typhoons go north. Typhoons go west. They do not sit in the Sargasso like a dog on a porch, but this one did.

The weather service later called it an "anomalous subtropical cyclonic event," which is a long way of saying they didn't know what it was either.

It found us Wednesday morning. The barometer dropped so fast I thought it was broken. The sky went from blue to yellow to a color I have no name for, a color like a bruise on fruit, and the wind came not gradually but all at once, as if someone had opened a door.

Wen was at the wheel. She turned us into it. You always turn into it.

---

There were four of us aboard. Wen. Me. Paulo Ferreira, our deckhand, twenty-three, who sent money home to his mother in Mindelo and collected those Japanese comic books, stacks of them in his bunk. And old Hassan, our engineer, who spoke four languages but preferred silence in all of them.

When the storm was six hours old and the swells were running fifteen feet, Wen called us together in the wheelhouse. The rain was horizontal. You couldn't hear yourself think, so she shouted.

She said: there is a shipping lane forty nautical miles northeast. If she sent the distress call now, someone might reach us by morning. Paulo and Hassan and I should get into the life raft. She would stay with the boat.

Paulo said, "Captain, that's—"

"That's my decision," Wen said. "And I'm not asking."

Hassan said nothing. He went below and came back with his sea bag and his prayer rug, and he got in the raft, and his face was the face of a man who understood something he wished he didn't. Paulo followed, crying, the rain hiding it but not really.

Wen looked at me.

I said, "I'll put the kettle on."

She didn't argue. I think she was grateful, though Wen was not the kind of person who said that word aloud. She just nodded once and turned back to the wheel.

I watched Hassan and Paulo go over the side. The raft inflated bright orange against that apocalypse sea. They were picked up nine hours later by a container ship out of Jacksonville. Paulo still sends me letters sometimes, neater than the bank's, and kinder.

---

Why did I stay?

I was fifty-seven years old. I had a bad hip and a pension that didn't exist and a sister in Recife who I spoke to twice a year on her birthday and mine. I had been on the *Mara Celeste* longer than I had been married, longer than I had been a mother — my son, Tomás, grown and gone to Lisbon, a stranger who called on Christmas with nothing to say. The boat was where my life had happened. Not all of it. But the parts that counted.

And Wen needed someone to bring her tea.

That's not a good enough reason. I know that. I've carried it for three years and I know it doesn't hold up in the rational light. But I'll tell you something: most of the things we do, the real things, the ones that make us who we are, don't hold up in the rational light. They hold up in the dark, when you're gripping a railing and the sea is trying to swallow you and someone you love is at the wheel and there's a kettle on the stove.

---

Wednesday night. The first night.

The pumps were still working then. The hull was groaning but holding, and the old ironwood planking flexed in ways that would have shattered fiberglass. Old Joaquim built his boats to bend, not break, and she bent, God how she bent, but she did not break. Not that night.

I made tea. Oolong, from a tin we'd bought in Bridgetown, leaves the color of tobacco. I brought it to the wheelhouse in the blue enamel mug with the chipped rim, the one Wen always used, and I wedged myself into the corner by the chart table and I watched her work.

She was extraordinary at the wheel. I never told her that. You don't tell Wen things like that; she'd look at you the way a dog looks at a ceiling fan. But her hands — brown, square, scarred across the knuckles from a hundred small repairs — they moved on the wheel the way Hassan's moved on his prayer beads, with a knowledge that lived below thought. She read the waves through the hull, through her feet, through whatever sixth sense God gives to people born on the water, and she turned into each one at exactly the right moment, taking the blow at the bow where the *Celeste* was strongest.

The tea went cold. It always went cold. In eleven years I don't think Wen drank a cup of tea while it was still hot. She'd take it hours later, stone cold, and drink it in one long swallow like medicine, and I'd think: this is the most stubborn woman alive.

---

Thursday. Day two.

At six in the morning the wind eased just enough for the sea to become something you could look at rather than merely endure, and I went to the galley and boiled water — the gas stove still worked, a miracle — and I made rice and scrambled the last four eggs and I set two places at the table and Wen came down and sat across from me and picked up the cards.

We played three hands of rummy. She won two. I won one, and only because she was distracted by a sound in the hull — a deep, resonant moan, like a cello played by someone who only knew sadness. She cocked her head and listened, the way you listen to a person, not a thing, and then she picked up her cards again and laid down three queens and said, "Gin."

"That's not how rummy works," I said.

"It is today," she said.

I gave her my banana. She peeled it with one hand, ate it in three bites, and went back to the wheel.

The hull kept singing.

---

Thursday afternoon, the number two pump failed.

Hassan would have fixed it in an hour. Without Hassan, it was a death sentence delivered politely, in the language of rising water. I went below with a flashlight and saw the bilge had risen to the engine mounts. The water was black and cold and it moved with the ship's roll like something alive, like something patient.

I went up and told Wen.

She nodded.

"How long?" I asked.

"Depends on the sea." She paused. "The planking's working open. Probably been working open for a year. I've been caulking her with prayer and pine tar." Another pause. "Mostly prayer."

"Wen."

"Dora."

"We could still call—"

"No."

She said it the way you close a door. Not hard. Just final.

---

Let me tell you what she did next, because this is the part the newspapers got wrong. They said she "lashed herself to the mast in a fit of mad determination." They made it sound like something from a painting — Odysseus and the sirens, a woman possessed.

It was nothing like that.

What happened was: Thursday evening, the wind came back worse than before, and the wheel was kicking so hard that Wen couldn't hold it alone. The cockpit was knee-deep in wash, and every wave that broke over the bow tried to pull her off her feet. She was exhausted. Two days without sleep. Her hands were raw and bleeding where the wheel spokes had torn the skin.

So she went to the mast — the little cargo mast just forward of the wheelhouse, where we rigged the boom for loading — and she took a length of line and she tied herself to it. Not dramatically. Not with any ceremony. She tied herself the way she tied everything: quickly, competently, with a bowline that wouldn't slip and wouldn't jamb. Then she went back to the wheel, and the line gave her purchase, gave her something to lean against when the sea tried to take her.

It was practical. It was the most practical thing I've ever seen.

I stood in the wheelhouse door and watched her — this small woman, five foot three, maybe a hundred and twenty pounds, roped to a mast in a typhoon — and what I thought was not, "She is brave," or "She is crazy." What I thought was: she looks like her grandfather. The jaw. The way she set her feet. Old Joaquim at the wheel of this same boat in 1983, the year of the winter gales, when I was a brand-new cook who couldn't tell port from starboard and thought the horizon was supposed to stay level.

---

Thursday night into Friday. The last night.

The water was up to my knees in the galley. I couldn't use the stove anymore. I found the last of the oolong in the tin, and I chewed the dry leaves and let the taste sit on my tongue — bitter, floral, the ghost of every cup I'd ever made — and I brought a handful to Wen at the wheel and she took them from my palm and put them in her mouth and chewed, and we stood there like two old goats working our cud in the end of the world.

The stars came out sometime around three in the morning. The eye, maybe, or something like it — a pause in the storm that let you see the sky, and the sky was so thick with stars it looked like someone had spilled salt on a black table. Wen looked up. I watched her look up. Her face was swollen from the wind and the salt, and her lips were cracked, and she had a cut above her left eye that had bled down into her eyebrow and dried black.

She said: "Dora, do you remember the time granddad dropped the anchor on his foot?"

I did. He'd hopped around the deck cursing in three languages while Beto — the cook before me — laughed so hard he fell into the hold.

"He loved this boat more than he loved people," Wen said. "I used to think that was a flaw."

"And now?"

She shrugged. The shrug of a woman who no longer needed to resolve anything.

"People leave," she said. "The boat just asks you to keep her afloat."

She looked at me with something I couldn't read. Apology, maybe. Acknowledgment.

"I'm sorry about the tea," she said.

"It was always cold anyway."

"I know. I liked it cold."

"You never told me that."

"Would you have stopped bringing it hot?"

"No."

"That's why I never told you."

---

Friday. Dawn.

I stood at the galley table, knee-deep in water now, and I dealt two hands of rummy. The cards were soaked. They stuck together and tore at the edges and the ink bled hearts into spades. I couldn't tell a king from a nine. Didn't matter. I laid them out in rows and played both hands and Wen won, because Wen always won, because even in absentia she knew what I was holding.

Above me, through the ceiling, through the cracked and weeping deck, I could hear her singing. Singing. A fado, one of the old ones, the ones old Joaquim used to sing when the engine wouldn't start and he needed to fill his hands with sound while they worked. I couldn't make out the words. Didn't need to. Fado doesn't live in its words. It lives in the space between them, in the breath the singer takes when the song is too heavy to carry and too precious to set down.

---

The hull opened at half past seven on Friday morning.

I felt it before I heard it — a shudder that went through the whole boat, through the soles of my feet and up my spine, the feeling of something that has been holding on finally letting go. Then the sound: a long, low exhalation, as if the *Mara Celeste* had been holding her breath for fifty-two years and had at last been given permission to stop.
